title: TN Visa Tax Filing Checklist: Complete 2026 Guide for Canadians Working in the US
description: Step-by-step TN visa tax filing checklist for Canadians working in the US. Covers residency status, treaty benefits, required forms, state taxes, and common mistakes that cost thousands.
content:
## Key Takeaways

- TN visa holders can choose resident or non-resident tax status—each has major implications
- The Canada-US tax treaty can save you $5,000-15,000 annually if used correctly
- You must file **both** US federal (1040/1040-NR) and Canadian T1 returns
- State tax obligations depend on where you work, not where your employer is based
- Most TN workers overpay by $3,000+ because they don't optimize cross-border taxes

## Understanding Your TN Visa Tax Status

As a TN visa holder working in the US, you're in a unique tax situation. Unlike H-1B workers, TN visa holders maintain strong ties to Canada—you likely return home frequently, keep Canadian bank accounts, and plan to eventually move back.

This creates a critical question: **Are you a US tax resident or non-resident?**

### The Substantial Presence Test

The IRS uses the **Substantial Presence Test (SPT)** to determine tax residency:

**You're a US resident if:**
- You were physically present in the US for 31+ days this year, AND
- The sum of days over 3 years ≥ 183 days using this formula:
  - All days this year × 1
  - Days last year × 1/3
  - Days 2 years ago × 1/6

**Example:**
- 2026: 200 days in US → 200 × 1 = 200
- 2025: 180 days in US → 180 × 1/3 = 60
- 2024: 150 days in US → 150 × 1/6 = 25
- **Total: 285 days → You ARE a US resident**

Use our [Substantial Presence Test Calculator](/us-canada-tax-calculator) to check your status instantly.

### Choosing Your Tax Status: Critical Decision

Even if the SPT says you're a resident, you can elect **non-resident status** using the Canada-US tax treaty (Form 8833).

**Resident Status Pros:**
- Lower tax rates (standard deduction + itemized deductions)
- Capital gains taxed at 0-20% instead of 30%
- No 30% withholding on interest/dividends
- Can claim spouse/dependents even if they live in Canada

**Resident Status Cons:**
- Must report worldwide income (including Canadian sources)
- No treaty benefits for Canadian employment income
- Canadian RRSP/TFSA become reportable foreign accounts
- Potential double taxation on Canadian assets

**Non-Resident Status Pros:**
- Only US-sourced income taxed
- Canadian income stays in Canada
- Simpler filing (1040-NR, not 1040)
- Easier to unwind when you return to Canada

**Non-Resident Status Cons:**
- No standard deduction ($14,600 lost)
- Capital gains/dividends taxed at 30% flat rate
- Can't claim Canadian spouse/kids as dependents

**Rule of Thumb:**
- **Choose Resident** if: You're married (Canadian spouse), have kids, or own Canadian investments
- **Choose Non-Resident** if: Single, plan to return to Canada within 2 years, keep most assets in Canada

Calculate which saves you more with our [free tax comparison tool](/us-canada-tax-calculator).

## Complete TN Visa Tax Filing Checklist

### Phase 1: Pre-Filing (January-February)

**✓ Determine Tax Residency Status**
- [ ] Count days in US using Substantial Presence Test
- [ ] Decide: File as resident (1040) or non-resident (1040-NR)?
- [ ] If choosing non-resident via treaty, prepare Form 8833

**✓ Gather Tax Documents (Due by January 31)**
- [ ] **W-2** from your US employer (wage/salary info)
- [ ] **1099-INT** (US interest income from banks)
- [ ] **1099-DIV** (US dividends/capital gains)
- [ ] **1099-B** (Stock sales—RSUs, ESPP, stock options)
- [ ] **1099-MISC** (Consulting/freelance income if applicable)
- [ ] **Canadian T4** (if you worked in Canada part of the year)
- [ ] **Canadian T5** (Canadian interest/dividends)
- [ ] **RRSP contribution receipts** (for Canadian tax credit)

**✓ Document Your Canadian Ties**
- [ ] Canadian driver's license and address
- [ ] Canadian bank account statements (all year)
- [ ] Property ownership docs (house/condo in Canada)
- [ ] Family ties (spouse/kids living in Canada)
- [ ] Professional memberships (CPA Canada, engineering colleges)

**Why?** If the IRS challenges your non-resident election, you need proof of "closer connection" to Canada.

### Phase 2: US Federal Tax Return (Due April 15)

**Option A: Filing as US Resident (Form 1040)**

**Step 1: Report All Income**
- [ ] Line 1a: W-2 wages from US employer
- [ ] Line 1z: Add-back of Canadian employment income (if any)
- [ ] Line 2b: Interest (US + Canadian banks)
- [ ] Line 3b: Dividends (US + Canadian stocks)

**Step 2: Claim Deductions**
- [ ] Line 12: Standard deduction ($14,600 single, $29,200 married)
- [ ] **OR** Schedule A: Itemized deductions (mortgage interest, state taxes up to $10k, charity)

**Step 3: Calculate Tax**
- [ ] Use tax tables (10% up to $11,600, then 12%, 22%, etc.)
- [ ] Add self-employment tax if you freelanced (Schedule SE)

**Step 4: Claim Credits**
- [ ] Foreign Tax Credit (Form 1116) for Canadian taxes paid
- [ ] Child Tax Credit ($2,000/child if dependents in Canada)
- [ ] Premium Tax Credit (if you bought health insurance on marketplace)

**Step 5: State Tax Return**
- [ ] File state return where you worked (due April 15-18 depending on state)
- [ ] Claim state tax credit for Canadian taxes if state allows

**Option B: Filing as Non-Resident (Form 1040-NR)**

**Step 1: Report US-Sourced Income Only**
- [ ] Line 1a: W-2 wages from US employer
- [ ] Line 1z: Capital gains from US stocks (1099-B)
- [ ] Line 2b: US interest (but NOT Canadian interest)

**Step 2: Attach Form 8833 (Treaty Election)**
- [ ] Check box "Article 15 - Income from Employment"
- [ ] Explain why you're electing non-resident status despite SPT
- [ ] Provide Canadian tax ID (SIN) and address

**Step 3: No Standard Deduction**
- Non-residents don't get the $14,600 deduction
- Can only deduct itemized deductions **directly connected to US income**
- Example: State income tax, charity to US orgs, mortgage interest on US property

**Step 4: Calculate Tax**
- Same tax rates as residents (10%, 12%, 22%, etc.)
- But you lose the standard deduction benefit

**Step 5: State Tax Return**
- [ ] File as non-resident (Form varies by state)
- [ ] Only report income earned in that state

### Phase 3: Canadian Tax Return (Due April 30 or June 15)

**Step 1: Determine Canadian Residency**
- [ ] Did you maintain residential ties (home, spouse, dependents)?
- [ ] If YES → File as **Canadian resident** (worldwide income)
- [ ] If NO → File as **non-resident** or **deemed non-resident**

**Step 2: Report Income**
- [ ] Line 10100: Employment income (Canadian T4 + US W-2 converted to CAD)
- [ ] Line 12100: Interest (Canadian + US, converted to CAD)
- [ ] Line 12000: Taxable capital gains

**Step 3: Claim Foreign Tax Credit**
- [ ] **Schedule 1, Line 40500**: Federal Foreign Tax Credit
- [ ] Use Form T2209 to calculate credit
- [ ] Attach US tax returns as proof of foreign tax paid

**Step 4: Provincial Tax**
- [ ] File provincial return (BC, ON, AB, etc.)
- [ ] Claim provincial foreign tax credit (separate from federal)

**Step 5: RRSP Contributions**
- [ ] Claim deduction (Line 20800) up to 18% of prior year income
- [ ] Contribution room carries forward if you don't use it all

### Phase 4: Foreign Asset Reporting

**US Side (If Filing 1040 as Resident):**

**FBAR - FinCEN Form 114** (Due April 15, auto-extension to Oct 15)
- [ ] Required if: Canadian bank accounts totaled >$10,000 USD any day
- [ ] Report ALL Canadian accounts (chequing, savings, RRSP, TFSA)
- [ ] File online at FinCEN website (separate from tax return)
- [ ] **Penalty for non-filing: $10,000-$100,000**

**Form 8938 - FATCA Statement** (Filed with 1040)
- [ ] Required if: $50k year-end OR $75k any day (single, living in US)
- [ ] Required if: $100k year-end OR $150k any day (married filing jointly)
- [ ] Report Canadian RRSP, TFSA, brokerage accounts
- [ ] **Penalty: $10,000 + $10,000/month after IRS notice**

**Form 8621 - PFIC Reporting** (If you own Canadian mutual funds/ETFs)
- [ ] Canadian mutual funds are "Passive Foreign Investment Companies"
- [ ] Must report each fund separately (can be 20+ forms!)
- [ ] Punitive tax treatment (no preferential capital gains rates)
- [ ] **Pro Tip:** Sell Canadian mutual funds, buy US ETFs instead

**Canadian Side:**

**Form T1135 - Foreign Income Verification** (Due with T1 return)
- [ ] Required if: You own >$100,000 CAD in foreign property
- [ ] Report US bank accounts, brokerage, 401(k), real estate
- [ ] **Penalty: $25/day late, max $2,500**

### Phase 5: State Tax Obligations

**Community Property States (CA, WA, TX, AZ, NV, NM, LA, ID, WI):**
- If you're married, 50% of your income belongs to your spouse (even if non-working)
- This affects filing status and income splitting

**No-Income-Tax States (AK, FL, NV, NH, SD, TN, TX, WA, WY):**
- You still file federal, just no state return
- Exception: NH taxes interest/dividends

**Reciprocal Agreement States:**
- If you live in one state but work in another, check for reciprocal agreements
- Example: DC ↔ MD ↔ VA (only file in resident state)

**High-Tax States to Watch:**
- **California:** 13.3% top rate, aggressive residency audits
- **New York:** 10.9% top rate + NYC tax (3.876%)
- **Massachusetts:** 5% flat rate but taxes non-residents on MA-sourced income

## Common TN Visa Tax Mistakes (That Cost Thousands)

### Mistake #1: Not Filing Form 8833 (Treaty Election)

**The Error:**
You pass the Substantial Presence Test (resident) but want to file as non-resident. You submit 1040-NR but forget Form 8833.

**The Cost:**
IRS rejects your return. You must file 1040 as resident, lose $14,600 standard deduction, and owe $3,200 more tax.

**The Fix:**
- **Always attach Form 8833** if electing treaty benefits
- Explain in Part III why you have a "closer connection" to Canada
- Provide Canadian address, SIN, and ties evidence

### Mistake #2: Paying 30% Withholding on Investment Income

**The Error:**
Your US brokerage withholds 30% on dividends because you said you're a non-resident alien.

**The Cost:**
$5,000 dividend → $1,500 withheld → You only get $3,500.

**The Fix:**
- File **Form W-8BEN** with your brokerage
- Claim reduced treaty rate (15% for dividends, 10% for interest)
- Savings: $750 on $5,000 dividend

### Mistake #3: Not Claiming Foreign Tax Credit

**The Error:**
You pay US tax on your W-2 income, then pay Canadian tax again. You don't claim FTC in Canada.

**The Cost:**
Double taxation: $80k income → $16k US tax + $28k Canadian tax = **$44k total** (55% effective rate!)

**The Fix:**
- Claim Foreign Tax Credit (Schedule 1, Line 40500) in Canada
- Offset US tax dollar-for-dollar
- Net Canadian tax: $28k - $16k = $12k
- **Effective rate: 35%** (saved $16,000!)

Use our [Foreign Tax Credit calculator](/us-canada-tax-calculator) to optimize your credit.

### Mistake #4: Forgetting State Tax When You Move

**The Error:**
You worked in California Jan-Jun, then moved to Washington (no state tax). You don't file CA return.

**The Cost:**
CA Franchise Tax Board issues an assessment for **full-year CA residency**.
- Demand: $8,500 CA tax + penalties
- Reality: You only owed $3,200 (6 months)

**The Fix:**
- File **CA Form 540-NR** (non-resident/part-year)
- Report only income earned Jan-Jun
- Prove you moved (WA driver's license, lease, utility bills)

### Mistake #5: TFSA Reporting Failure

**The Error:**
You're a US tax resident but keep contributing to your Canadian TFSA. You don't report it.

**The Cost:**
- TFSA is a "foreign trust" to the IRS
- Requires Form 3520 (foreign trust reporting)
- **Penalty: 35% of TFSA balance** for non-filing
- Plus FBAR penalty: $10,000

**The Fix:**
- Stop contributing to TFSA while US resident
- Consider closing TFSA and moving funds to RRSP (treaty-protected)
- File Form 3520 for all prior years (catch-up)

## Real-World Example: TN Visa Tax Filing

**Profile:**
- Sarah, 32, software engineer from Vancouver
- TN visa working in Seattle, WA (no state tax)
- Salary: $140,000 USD
- Kept condo in Vancouver, flies home every 2 weeks
- Days in US: 210 (passes SPT → resident)
- Canadian RRSP: $80,000 CAD, TFSA: $40,000 CAD

**Tax Strategy: Elect Non-Resident Status**

Why? Sarah plans to return to Canada in 2027. Filing as resident would require:
- Reporting Canadian condo rental income
- FBAR and Form 8938 (RRSP + TFSA)
- Form 3520 (TFSA foreign trust reporting)
- Paying US tax on Canadian investment gains

**US Filing (1040-NR):**
- Income: $140,000 W-2
- Deductions: $0 (no standard deduction for non-residents)
- Taxable income: $140,000
- Federal tax: $27,752
- Form 8833: Claim Article 15 treaty benefit (employment income)

**Canadian Filing (T1 as Resident):**
- Income: $140,000 USD × 1.36 FX = $190,400 CAD
- RRSP contribution: $10,000 CAD (saves $3,500 tax)
- Provincial tax (BC): $12,850
- Federal tax: $38,205
- Foreign Tax Credit: -$27,752 USD × 1.36 = -$37,743 CAD
- **Net Canadian tax: $13,312 CAD**

**Total Tax Paid:**
- US: $27,752 USD
- Canada: $13,312 CAD ÷ 1.36 = $9,788 USD
- **Combined: $37,540 (26.8% effective rate)**

**Compared to No Optimization:**
- If Sarah filed as US resident: $32,000 US + $18,000 CAD = **$50,000 total**
- **Savings: $12,460** by choosing non-resident status + FTC optimization

## Software vs CPA: What's Right for You?

**DIY Tax Software (TurboTax, H&R Block, Sprintax):**
- **Cost:** $50-$200
- **Pros:** Fast, cheap, handles basic W-2 + 1040 situations
- **Cons:** Can't handle complex cross-border scenarios, no treaty elections

**Cross-Border Tax CPA:**
- **Cost:** $2,500-$5,000/year
- **Pros:** Expert advice, handles complex situations, audit defense
- **Cons:** Expensive, slow (6-8 week turnaround), overkill for simple cases

**TaxBridge Calculator + Filing:**
- **Cost:** Free calculator, $49 guided filing (coming soon)
- **Pros:** Cross-border optimized, FTC calculator, treaty elections, instant results
- **Cons:** Not full-service (you still file yourself)

**When You NEED a CPA:**
- Self-employment income >$50k
- Real estate in both countries
- Business ownership (corp, LLC, partnership)
- Green card application pending (scrutiny)
- Prior tax issues or unfiled returns

**When DIY Works:**
- Simple W-2 + RSU income
- No rental properties
- No foreign trusts (TFSA reporting)
- Comfortable following a checklist

## Timeline: When to File What

**January 15, 2027**
- Q4 2026 estimated tax payment (if you owe >$1,000)

**January 31, 2027**
- Receive W-2 from employer
- Receive 1099s (interest, dividends, stock sales)

**February 28, 2027**
- Canadian T4 slips available on CRA My Account

**April 15, 2027** (or April 18 if falls on weekend)
- **US federal tax return** (1040 or 1040-NR)
- **State tax return** (varies by state)
- **FBAR deadline** (auto-extension to Oct 15)

**April 30, 2027** (or next business day)
- **Canadian T1 return** (if employee)

**June 15, 2027**
- **Canadian T1 return** (if self-employed)
- **US federal return** (if you lived abroad full year—auto 2-month extension)

**October 15, 2027**
- Extension deadline for US returns (must file Form 4868 by April 15)

## Action Items: Your TN Visa Tax Checklist

**Before Year-End:**
- [ ] Count days in US (use Substantial Presence Test calculator)
- [ ] Decide: File as resident or non-resident?
- [ ] Maximize RRSP contributions (deadline March 1 for prior year)
- [ ] Review Canadian ties (address, driver's license, bank accounts)

**January-February:**
- [ ] Gather all tax documents (W-2, 1099s, T4, T5)
- [ ] Decide on tax software or CPA
- [ ] File Form W-8BEN with US brokerages (reduce withholding)

**March-April:**
- [ ] File US 1040/1040-NR by April 15
- [ ] File state return by April 15-18
- [ ] File Canadian T1 by April 30 (or June 15 if self-employed)
- [ ] Claim Foreign Tax Credit in Canada
- [ ] File FBAR if Canadian accounts >$10k
- [ ] File Form 8938 if threshold met

**Ongoing:**
- [ ] Track days in US monthly (for next year's residency determination)
- [ ] Save 30-40% of income for taxes (both countries)
- [ ] Review treaty position annually (changes if you get green card)
